title: Chloe Moffat: Dad of woman who took her own life says Treasury failed in its duty of care
description: The father of a civil service employee who took her own life the day after a meeting with her managers has said the lack of support given to her by th
body: The father of a civil service employee who took her own life the day after a meeting with her managers has said the lack of support given to her by the Treasury "beggars belief".Chloe Moffat, 26, a personal assistant to a Treasury director, died on 20 May last year, after she was told of allegations she had shared sensitive confidential information about colleagues, which she denied.Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today programme, David Moffat said he did not feel the Treasury had taken responsibility for its part in her death.He added that her loss was "devastating", and had "torn such a big hole in our lives".The Treasury said "it will learn the lessons from this tragedy".On 19 May 2025, Chloe went to what she thought was a routine one-to-one with her line manager, but a more senior manager was also present."Chloe's first comment was, 'Oh, this must be serious, there's two of you here'", David told Today's Emma Barnett. "So that's the first time that she was aware of anything [that] might be a to do.""And then they worked through and put several allegations to her that she'd shared confidential information."During the meeting, David said she had asked on several occasions if she would lose her job, and if she could have a friend there - both of which were refused.A coroner found at an inquest earlier in August that the Treasury did not apply written disciplinary policy, which would have made clear that if the allegations against Chloe were proven, the likely penalty was a written warning, not dismissal."Even though she asked, they said they could not determine the outcome," David said.Straight after the meeting, Chloe was locked out of her emails. "That was all part of the shock and awe of it all for Chloe," David said.The coroner found that the meeting between Chloe and her managers "materially contributed" to her death.David said that "there wasn't any duty of care" shown to Chloe by the Treasury."There was no safeguarding, there was no support during or after that meeting, from what we've seen and what we've read", he said."It beggars belief that an organisation that is front and central in our government cannot get it right."Asked whether he felt the Treasury had taken responsibility for its part in her death, he answered: "Not yet".He added, however, that he and his wife had received a letter on Tuesday from the Treasury's permanent secretary, James Bowler, and that they had also met him last August.David said while they could not change what happened to Chloe, he wanted "to ensure" that "lessons are learned". "If something positive can come from this unbearable loss that we're suffering, that's all we look to achieve."He said he and his wife Anne were unsure if they would be pursuing further action against the Treasury, but that they wanted "redress".A spokesperson for the Treasury said: "The Treasury's deepest sympathies continue to be with Chloe's friends and family, and the department continues to mourn our colleague. "We will learn the lessons from this tragedy. We are working urgently to respond to the coroner's findings and we have introduced immediate changes to our guidance, support and wellbeing arrangements.  "Chloe's parents have agreed to meet with us so we can hear their views and update on actions the department is taking."If you have been affected by any of the issues in this story, help and support is available at BBC Action Line.

schema.headline: Chloe Moffat: Dad of woman who took her own life says Treasury failed in its duty of care

title: NHS failing child sexual abuse victims, say psychiatrists
description: People sexually abused as children who seek help in later life for mental health problems are being failed by the NHS, senior doctors have told the BB
body: People sexually abused as children who seek help in later life for mental health problems are being failed by the NHS, senior doctors have told the BBC.The Royal College of Psychiatrists is issuing a public apology for what it says is decades of mismanagement and misdiagnosis in the UK.For some, it has worsened their traumas, it said.The college said mental health staff have been too focussed on treating symptoms rather than exploring how past traumatic experiences can still affect patients.Support is improving, it said, but there must be better training and more investment - something NHS bosses have said is being introduced.The apology has been included in a report, external by the college and given to the BBC.Immediate past president of the college, Dr Lade Smith, said she was "sorry" that, too often, victims have suffered "avoidable harm when seeking help".The report details how treatment has sometimes been inappropriate, while people have been re-traumatised by the experience of repeated assessments and history-taking and not always being believed.Dr Smith told the BBC it was clear people were not getting the support they needed, and that this was not just a failing of psychiatrists, but the whole mental health system."Services are so fragmented. The system is set up to provide short, discreet episodes of care. Psychiatrists do not get the time to build up a relationship with patients so they can be properly supported."They are lucky if they get eight sessions of therapy, when it could take eight sessions for a person just to disclose the abuse."And these are just the people who get support – many don't even get seen by mental health services because services are so stretched," she said.Estimates suggest nearly one in 10 adults in England and Wales were sexually abused in childhood.Such trauma increases the risk of mental health problems, including alcohol and drug misuse, eating disorders, self-harm, complex PTSD, anxiety and depression.Many struggle to talk about the abuse. Around two-thirds of those abused as children have not disclosed it to services by the time they reach adulthood.One in five never disclose, and many of those that do take decades to speak out.Caroline Thompson, 65, is someone who feels let down by the NHS.She was psychologically and sexually abused when she was a child. She went on to raise a family and have a successful career as a specialist ear, nose and throat doctor.It was not until she started experiencing terrifying nightmares, aged 55, that left her unable to function due to mental exhaustion and lack of sleep, that she realised she needed help and was referred to mental health services.The apology comes after the college set up a working group of experts, doctors and abuse survivors, including Caroline and chaired by leading consultant psychiatrists Jo Stubley and Maria Podlejska-Eyres, to review NHS care.The group was set up after mental health services have seen a rise in people coming forward seeking help in the last decade or so, following high-profile abuse scandals involving schools, children's homes and religious institutions, as well as the Jimmy Savile crimes.The college is calling for a number of changes. It is promising to develop specialist training materials for psychiatrists, but wants mandatory training for all mental health staff on the importance of trauma-informed care for survivors of child sex abuse.And it has recommended national guidance be published on how to recognise and respond to disclosures of historic child sex abuse, as well as an overhaul of services so those needing help can get the long-term support they need.Gabrielle Shaw, chief executive of the National Association for People Abused in Childhood, said this was a "significant and welcome" apology, but it must lead to "meaningful change"."For too many adult survivors, mental health services have not felt like a route to safety or recovery." A spokesman for NHS England said specialist services were available, highlighting how victims could access support 24 hours a day, seven days a week through sexual assault referral centres and counselling services with information about them available on the NHS website, external."People who have suffered historic child sexual abuse may not have spoken about it for years, so it's vital they know they can access specialist, trauma-informed support through the NHS," he added.He also said steps were being taken to better support children and young people with additional training being provided to mental health support teams in schools and colleges.If you've been affected by the issues in this story, you can find information, advice and support from the BBC's Action Line. Anyone feeling emotionally distressed or suicidal can call Samaritans for free on 116 123 or visit samaritans.org in the UK.

schema.headline: NHS failing child sexual abuse victims, say psychiatrists

title: As Ukraine hits Russia's refineries, Russia targets Ukraine's petrol pumps
description: "Fill up quickly and move on," Mayor Ihor Terekhov warns drivers in Ukraine's second largest city Kharkiv.Two petrol stations in the city in Ukraine's
body: "Fill up quickly and move on," Mayor Ihor Terekhov warns drivers in Ukraine's second largest city Kharkiv.Two petrol stations in the city in Ukraine's north-east were hit by Russian drones on Monday, which local officials say wounded two people. In another attack on a petrol station outside the city of Kryvyi Rih last week, three people were killed.Russia's campaign of targeting civilian filling stations with drones and missiles began in earnest in April, primarily in regions on the front line, and the attacks are steadily growing more frequent.At the same time, Russia has endured two waves of severe fuel shortages across the country as a result of Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian oil refineries.In total, Russia has hit at least 246 filling stations across Ukraine so far, says Oleksandr Sirenko, an analyst with Ukrainian energy think-tank Nafto Rynok ("Oil Market").In July alone, the Centre for Information Resilience, an open-source investigation non-profit group, verified 114 Russian strikes on filling stations, compared with 66 the month before.Given the threat, police have issued special guidance urging motorists to leave petrol stations and, if necessary, to abandon their vehicles whenever air raid alerts sound. "You can fix your car, but you won't get your life back," says one police force in the Dnipropetrovsk region.The damage is highly disruptive and puts civilians at considerable risk.According to Sirenko, initially the attacks were being carried out with smaller, remote-controlled drones, but then Russia started using bigger, more expensive and more destructive Iranian-made Shahed drones.One Shahed drone is estimated to cost between $20,000 (£14,500) and $50,000 (£36,000)."One petrol station took five Shahed hits," Sirenko tells the BBC. "These Shaheds cost more than the petrol station."Some key roads have no functioning petrol stations left, such as the road linking the two major cities of Kharkiv and Dnipro.All the petrol stations have been destroyed around Opishnya, a large village in neighbouring Poltava region."You can see our enemy's strategy. They want to deprive us of fuel," says village chief Mykola Riznyk. In a video on Facebook, he says local authorities have begun stocking up on fuel, keeping small amounts of it in different locations.In Mykolaiv in southern Ukraine, local resident and driver Kateryna Stokolya says petrol stations everywhere are becoming far stricter about not working during air alerts."Now everyone's making allowances for that, and it's not a problem," she tells the BBC. "Security comes first. If you can't fill up now, you'll fill up later. There are no queues or panic buying."Stokolya believes that, in carrying out attacks of this nature, Russia's intended goal is "terrorising the public so we force the government to capitulate or accept agreements that do not favour Ukraine".In Ukrainian-controlled areas of the partly occupied Kherson region, almost half the petrol stations have stopped working. The others get attacked by Russian drones "almost every day", says deputy regional administration head Oleksandr Tolokonnikov.All petrol stations have reportedly been destroyed in Trostyanets, a town of almost 20,000 people near the north-eastern border with Russia. In response, local authorities started dispensing fuel straight from road tankers which keep changing their location to minimise the chances of being hit.Ukrainians appear to be heeding the advice of authorities."Clients aren't browsing the aisles anymore, looking at what we've got on our shelves," says Oleksandr Melnychuk, head of the strategic marketing department at BRSM Nafta chain of petrol stations. "They fill up and are keen to get on their way as soon as possible."His company has lost eight petrol stations and is rebuilding another two after they were hit.To protect customers, BRSM Nafta has been building concrete shelters at its forecourts and also covering them in anti-drone nets. It has also shortened working hours and reduced the number of staff present in some locations.However, so far the drone strikes have not had a dramatic impact on fuel supplies. According to a report by the National Bank of Ukraine, 4% of the country's filling stations have been damaged or destroyed, but the impact on the market has been small."Increasing sales in regions which are further away from the front line or from the border with Russia have made up for sales lost at destroyed stations," the report says.The picture in Russia is very different, after Ukraine's campaign of attacks on Russian refineries and other infrastructure.Russia has seen fuel shortages in almost every region as a result. One popular newspaper in Russia, Izvestia, said last week that petrol was only available at 28% of Russian filling stations.Unlike in Russia, Ukraine does not rely on vulnerable large refineries and fuel depots, instead importing fuel by road using tanker trucks.Ukraine's market is also saturated with numerous petrol stations, which usually offer drivers alternatives should one or several of them be targeted in a particular area, Sirenko says."You curse and drive on to another petrol station. OK, you travel for 10km more than you bargained for, but that's not such a big problem," he says.If anything, it is the war between the US and Iran that is having a bigger impact on local fuel prices, he says. Normally, the most expensive parts of filling stations are left undamaged by Russian attacks, such as petrol and diesel tanks underground.

schema.headline: As Ukraine hits Russia's refineries, Russia targets Ukraine's petrol pumps

title: Dolly Parton obituary: The country legend who sang from the heart
description: Dolly Parton: Life of the music legend whose songs touched millionsFigure caption, Dolly Parton: The life of a legendary country singerByTiffany Werth
body: Dolly Parton: Life of the music legend whose songs touched millionsFigure caption, Dolly Parton: The life of a legendary country singerByTiffany Wertheimer and Emma PetrieDolly Parton, the country singer from the Smoky Mountains of Tennessee, will be remembered for her songs that told beautiful stories so honestly, such as Coat of Many Colors, Jolene and I Will Always Love You.In a seven-decade career, Parton won 10 Grammy awards, sold more than 100 million records worldwide, and wrote in excess of 3,000 songs.Parton took her writing seriously, and considered herself a songwriter over everything else. "It's my way of expressing myself," she said. "It's my therapy.”She was also a savvy businesswoman who wasn't afraid to make tough decisions. Armed with a quick wit and southern charm, she took control of her showbusiness career that spanned more than 60 years.Image source, Getty Images/Michael Ochs ArchivesImage caption, Dolly Parton aged nineDolly Rebecca Parton was born in 1946, the fourth of 12 children, into a poor farming family who lived in a one-bedroom cabin in Tennessee.   Her father, Robert Lee Parton, was a tobacco farmer and paid a missionary a sack of cornmeal for delivering her.There was already music in the family - her mother, Avie Lee, sang folk songs all the time and her aunt played the guitar and wrote songs. During some of Parton's earliest performances, her uncle, Bill Owens, accompanied her on the guitar - formative years for the future music legend.From the age of six, she sang in the local church where her grandfather was the pastor, and was performing on her local TV station by the time she was a teenager.In 1959, when she was 13 years old, Parton performed with Uncle Bill at the Grand Ole Opry in Nashville - a live broadcast that is regarded as country music's biggest stage.She was introduced by Johnny Cash and received three encores.Image source, Getty Images//Michael Ochs ArchivesImage caption, Nineteen-year-old Dolly Parton in Nashville, 1965The 'town tramp'During her teenage years, Parton began to model herself on a local character who was known as the “town tramp”.  The lady wore bright red nail polish, low-cut tops and high heels - young Dolly thought she was beautiful.  When people said to her: “She ain’t nothing but trash”, Parton would reply: "Well, that’s what I’m gonna be when I grow up”.Parton sang “I’m just a backwoods Barbie / too much make-up, too much hair”, but her image was both a coat of armour and an astute disguise that helped get her noticed in showbusiness. She would get ahead of the jokes by making them first, and had a quick and simple response for anyone who suggested she should tone it down: "Go to hell."Image source, Getty Images/CBS photo ArchiveImage caption, Parton said she felt better in bright colours and shiny clothes on stage: "You'd be surprised how much it costs to look this cheap"After graduating from high school in 1964, she moved to Nashville to launch her singing career and met her future husband, Carl Dean, on her very first day.They married two years later and remained together until his death in 2025.In Nashville, Parton's singing caught the eye of country performer Porter Wagoner, who hired her to perform on his television programme.Over the next seven years, the pair became one of country music's most popular duos, releasing so many duets that many fans assumed they were a couple.But their relationship was a complicated one, and as Parton's solo career started to rise, so did tensions behind the scenes.Writing in her book Star of the Show: My Life on Stage, Parton said Wagoner saw her success away from his show as a "threat".Image source, Getty Images/Michael Ochs ArchivesImage caption, Dolly Parton with Porter Wagoner on the set of his TV show in 1967While travelling with Wagoner on a tour bus in 1969, Parton wrote Coat of Many Colors, a beautifully emotive tale of how she grew up poor, but rich with love. Scrawled on the back of one of Wagoner's dry cleaning receipts, it was rated by Rolling Stone magazine, external as her second best-ever song. Years later, Parton named her own children's book Coat of Many Colors, and it was the name of a 2015 TV movie based on her life."It's a song that's just stood by me... it's created a life of many colours for me," she said.Image source, Getty Images/Ethan MillerImage caption, Dolly Parton won several awards for her made-for-TV movie Coat of Many Colors'Sad little country song'Despite being unable to read sheet music, Parton played several instruments including the banjo, harp, piano and saxophone.She had her first number one hit - and first Grammy nomination - with the song Joshua in 1971 and finally left The Porter Wagoner Show in 1974 to concentrate on her solo career.To say goodbye to him, she wrote I Will Always Love You, a song that many think is about two lovers parting ways."That's the prettiest song I ever heard," Wagoner cried when he first heard it, her website says.The same year, Elvis Presley was set to record a cover of the song, but Parton pulled the deal when his manager demanded half of the songwriting rights.She cried all night at the difficult decision, and Priscilla Presley later told her that Elvis sang the song to her during their divorce.In 1992, Whitney Houston transformed it into a now-iconic power ballad. Parton said she was driving when she first heard the cover and had to pull over: “When I heard her go from the a cappella into the music part, I honestly thought I was going to have a heart attack, it was one of the most overwhelming things.”Houston's cover of Parton's “sad little country song” was one of the proudest moments of her life, she said.Parton re-recorded the song for The Best Little Whorehouse in Texas, a 1982 film in which she starred and was nominated for a Golden Globe for best actress.That other womanAnother of her most famous songs was released in 1974 - Jolene.Showing her aching vulnerability, it's about a bank clerk with flaming locks of auburn hair who flirted with her husband."Jolene, I'm begging of you, please don't take my man," she pleads.Parton said her husband, who was notoriously private, was a bit embarrassed by the song. But it was nothing serious - just a running joke between them: "I was saying, 'Hell, you're spending a lot of time at the bank. I don't believe we've got that kind of money.'"The song has been covered by many artists including The White Stripes, Miley Cyrus and Beyoncé, who changed up the lyrics to the more ominous: "I'm warning you, don't come for my man." In the years to come, Dolly Parton's success only grew, with more hits, nominations and awards - she won her first Grammy in 1978 for Here You Come Again. Image source, Richard McCaffrey/Michael Ochs ArchiveImage caption, "If you see someone without a smile, give 'em one of yours": Parton performing in California in 1978Playing her acrylic nailsIt was the theme song that Dolly Parton wrote for the 1980 movie 9 to 5 that fully propelled her to stardom.Actress Jane Fonda, who produced and starred in the film about women being discriminated against in the workplace, made a deal with Parton - she'd star in the film if she could also write the theme song.Realising her nails clicking together sounded like a typewriter, she wrote 9 to 5 while waiting around on set. Fonda said she realised straight away that it wasn't just a theme song - it was an anthem.The film was a big success at the box office and the song won several awards, including a Golden Globe.Image source, Getty Images/Michael Ochs ArchivesImage caption, Jane Fonda, Lily Tomlin and Dolly Parton in a scene from 9 to 5'I look like a woman but I think like a man'Parton was a successful and shrewd businesswoman, and in 2022 was listed by Forbes as one of America's richest self-made women, external."I look like a woman but I think like a man. I've done business with men who think I'm as silly as I look. By the time they realise I'm not, I've got the money and gone," she once said.Her physical appearance - the costumes, wigs, long painted nails and high heels - were merely a facade of a stereotypical “dumb blonde”. But she always said she knew she wasn't dumb "and I also know that I'm not blonde".She had her own record label, Dolly Records, and co-owned The Dollywood Company, which manages entertainment venues, a theme park, a water park and a resort.In 1986, she opened her Dollywood amusement park in the foothills of her beloved Smoky Mountains. As well as rollercoasters, it is home to the largest sanctuary for non-releasable bald eagles in the world. Its rehabilitation and breeding work has won awards and in 2007, the bald eagle was removed from the endangered species list.Image source, Ron Galella, Ltd./Ron Galella Collection via Getty ImagesImage caption, Parton, pictured at Dollywood in 1993, said she wanted to build a place where the culture of the Smoky Mountains could be celebratedDespite her wealth and success, Parton remained humble and supported the communities where she grew up.Inspired by her father who couldn’t read or write, she launched the Imagination Library in 1999, which gave free books to children in Tennessee. It has since expanded to Australia, the UK, Ireland and Canada, sending out millions of free books every year.Her non-profit organisation, The Dollywood Foundation, has funded scholarships, hospitals and donated to flood and wildfire victims.In 2020, as the Covid-19 pandemic gripped the world, Parton donated $1m (£716,000) to the Vanderbilt University Medical Centre which helped to fund the Moderna vaccine. In later years, Parton had to postpone or cancel several shows for health treatment.In May 2026, she postponed an upcoming Las Vegas residency because of treatment for kidney stones, saying it would take some time to heal and be "stage-performance ready"."I can't be dizzy carrying around banjos, guitars and such on five-inch heels - and you know that I'm going to be wearing them," she said in a video message. "Not to mention all those heavy rhinestone outfits, the big hair, my big... uh, personality," she joked.Image source, Brandon Sloter/Image Of Sport/Getty ImagesImage caption, Parton amazed fans when she performed at the NFL Thanksgiving half-time show in 2023, aged 77Parton spoke graciously throughout her career with humour and intelligence. She steered clear of politics, saying she didn't want to alienate half her audience. She was a courageous and talented trailblazer for country music at a time when women were not taken seriously in the industry, especially as solo artists.Parton said she hoped to be remembered for her songwriting and as somebody who took her work seriously, but not herself.She once offered this advice: “Never ignore your roots, your home, or your hair."It's guidance that she stayed true to throughout her life.

schema.headline: Dolly Parton obituary: The country legend who sang from the heart

title: CIA chief travels to Moscow for unannounced talks, US media reports
description: The head of the US Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) has travelled to Moscow for unannounced talks, the BBC's US news partner CBS has reported.John Ra
body: The head of the US Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) has travelled to Moscow for unannounced talks, the BBC's US news partner CBS has reported.John Ratcliffe reportedly arrived in the Russian capital earlier on Tuesday. Neither Washington or Moscow have confirmed the nature of the visit or who he was due to meet.In-person talks between high-level American and Russian officials are rare.Flight tracking data confirmed a large US military aircraft travelled to Russia from the US via Latvia on Tuesday. It departed later on Tuesday.BBC News has contacted the CIA, the White House and Pentagon for comment. Footage posted on social media showed the C-17 transport plane approaching Moscow's Vnukovo international airport.It departed Riga airport at 05:50 GMT and appeared to have landed in the Russian capital at around 07:04 GMT, according to data from FlightRadar24. It returned to Riga shortly before 17:00 GMT.Footage on social media also purported to show a diplomatic motorcade travelling through Moscow.Ahead of the trip, the US told Ukraine that a senior delegation would be travelling to Moscow and asked Kyiv to suspend strikes until they had left, a senior Ukrainian official told CBS.The trip is thought to be Ratcliffe's first trip to Russia as CIA director, although he has maintained contact with his intelligence counterparts in Moscow.John Foreman, who served as a British military attaché to Moscow between 2019 and 2022, told Radio 4's PM programme that the visit could be focused on "escalation management" given speculation recent drone activity in Germany could be linked to Russia.He said: "The Americans don't normally send such a high ranking official to Moscow unannounced at short notice unless something is up."Foreman said the trip could also concern the release of US detainees currently being held in Russia.Ratcliffe played a role in negotiations for the release of Russian-American citizen Ksenia Karelina, who was jailed in Russia for over a year after being accused of providing support to Ukraine. The CIA was also involved in a 2024 prisoner swap deal with Russia that saw the release of Wall Street Journal reporter Evan Gershkovich, as well as former US marine Paul Whelan and Russian-American journalist Alsu Kurmasheva.The US has had strained relations with Russia since it launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Since then, Russia has been isolated on the world stage and faced international economic sanctions.Ratcliffe appears to be one of the highest-ranking US officials to visit the country during President Donald Trump's second term.Trump met Russian President Vladimir Putin at a summit in Alaska last year but the meeting did not lead to a breakthrough. Subsequent US-led peace talks between Russia and Ukraine appear to have stalled.Additional reporting by Washington correspondent Daniel Bush and BBC Verify

schema.headline: CIA chief travels to Moscow for unannounced talks, US media reports

title: Raheem Sterling charged with dangerous driving after crash on M3 in Hampshire
description: Raheem Sterling will appear in court next month to face charges of dangerous driving and possessing nitrous oxide for wrongful inhalation after crashi
body: Raheem Sterling will appear in court next month to face charges of dangerous driving and possessing nitrous oxide for wrongful inhalation after crashing his car into motorway barriers in May.The former England winger, who most recently played for Feyenoord in the Dutch Eredivisie, crashed his Lamborghini into barriers on the M3 in Hampshire on the morning of Thursday, 28 May.The 31-year-old was arrested and then released on bail pending further enquiries.A Hampshire & Isle of Wight Constabulary spokesman said: "A driver will appear in court next month to face charges following a collision on the M3."Raheem Sterling, 31, from Berkshire, has been charged for the following offences: dangerous driving, possession of nitrous oxide for wrongful inhalation, failing to provide a specimen."The charges come following a single vehicle collision, involving a Lamborghini, on the M3 southbound, close to the Minley Interchange [Hampshire], on 28 May, 2026."No other vehicles were involved and no injuries were reported. Mr Sterling is due to appear at Basingstoke magistrates court on 15 September."Police suspected Sterling of "driving a vehicle whilst unfit through drugs," but that has not been included in the charges.In May a source close to Sterling told BBC Sport there was "no proof" of drugs in his system.The source added the player had faced "an extremely tough couple of years" and had been made to "feel worthless" and "forgotten about".Sterling has been without a club since leaving Dutch side Feyenoord at the end of last season.He joined Feyenoord in February on a short-term contract after leaving Chelsea by mutual consent.Chelsea paid £47.5m to sign Sterling from Manchester City in 2022, where he had won four Premier League titles, five League Cups and one FA Cup in seven years.In 2024 the former Liverpool winger joined Arsenal on loan, but upon returning to Chelsea in 2025 was exiled from the first-team squad and made to train separately.Sterling earned 82 England caps between 2012 and 2022, and appeared at three World Cups and two European Championships.

schema.headline: Raheem Sterling charged with dangerous driving after crash on M3 in Hampshire

title: Newspaper headlines: 'We will always love you, Dolly'
description: Perhaps unsurprisingly there's one person who appears on almost all of the front pages - Dolly Parton.The Sun, external, the Daily Mirror, external an
body: Perhaps unsurprisingly there's one person who appears on almost all of the front pages - Dolly Parton.The Sun, external, the Daily Mirror, external and the Daily Star, external all share the headline: "We will always love you, Dolly".  To the i Paper, external she was the "legendary queen of country",  who wanted to be "remembered as a songwriter". The Guardian, external leaves little doubt about whether she achieved that, noting she was "so gifted that she wrote two of the 20th century's greatest songs - Jolene and I Will Always Love You - in a single day"."Burnham warned of impending Russian UK attack" declares the Daily Mail, external on its front page.  It says the prime minister has been told by security experts to be prepared for a "direct response" from Moscow, over the UK's support for Ukraine.  The former Conservative defence minister, Tobias Elwood, tells the Daily Express, external Russia will seek to "exact a price".The Financial Times leads, external on China's criticism of fresh US sanctions, which aim to isolate Iran's economy.  The paper says any attempt to expand the sanctions regime to Chinese companies "would risk retaliation from Beijing".  The FT points out that President Xi Jinping is due to meet Donald Trump in Washington next month.According to the Times, external, Andy Burnham is poised to announce sanctions on Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank - despite warnings from within his party that the measure could spiral into a "de facto boycott" of Israel itself.  The government tells the paper it won't comment on "speculation", and that the foreign secretary "has been clear that illegal settlements threaten the viability of a Palestinian state and undermine security for both Israelis and Palestinians".The Daily Telegraph reports, external that Birmingham, once regarded as the "motor capital of Britain", is set to become England's first 20mph city.  It says the council, led by coalition of the Green Party, Liberal Democrats and Independents, want to introduce the speed restriction on all routes other than A-roads. The opposition, led by Reform UK, calls it an "anti motorist policy". A spokesperson for the local authority tells the paper: "Our message is simple: slower is safer."

schema.headline: Newspaper headlines: 'We will always love you, Dolly'

title: Back to school: How parents can save on uniform costs
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByJemma CrewBusiness reporter Back to school can stir up many emotions for parents, including anxiety about the extra costs
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByJemma CrewBusiness reporter Back to school can stir up many emotions for parents, including anxiety about the extra costs it brings.Almost half of parents said they're worried about the cost of school uniforms, according to research by the charity Save the Children and the Baby Bank Alliance network.And a third of the 2,000 parents polled said they've sacrificed things for themselves to meet back-to-school costs like uniforms, bags or books.New rules limiting the number of items branded with a school logo to three per child come into force in September, aimed at helping ease the financial burden.From baby banks to council grants, here are ways parents can ease the cost of kitting out their kids for school.Your first port of callSave the Children said the new uniform rules are a "good start" but back-to-school costs remain a concern for families across almost all income brackets.The government said schools should make second-hand uniforms accessible to parents."Speak to a teacher you trust, and explain that the costs are difficult," said Megan Meek-O'Connor, head of England and Westminster at Save the Children.Many schools have uniform hubs, swap shops and sales just before term starts, and hardship funds.In London, the School Uniform Reuse Network launched earlier this year, giving schools practical advice to start or improve their own swap shops. During its first term of operation, it saw more than 1,500 items reused across 24 schools.Don't dismiss baby banksParents of older children may not realise a so-called baby bank can help them, but many of the 400 support hubs across the UK provide uniforms for children up to and through secondary school.In its latest survey of members, the Baby Bank Alliance found school uniform was reported as a priority item for the first time.Late summer is one of the busiest times for Little Stars Shrewsbury - just over half the children helped since June have been given uniform support.Image source, Little Stars ShropshireImage caption, Boys' black and grey school trousers sorted into boxes at Little Stars ShropshireHannah Stoddart, operations manager at Little Stars Shrewsbury, said families come to them in varying circumstances. A child starting school might need fully kitting out, while an older pupil may just need to replace one or two items.Stoddart stressed that while the summer holidays "take their toll", the charity provides help all year."So when they've had that growth spurt, when they've scuffed their shoes or they've ripped their trousers or they need a winter coat, that's something they can come back to us for as well," she said.Supermarkets and pre-loved itemsThe relaxed rules on uniform branding mean parents can purchase more items from supermarkets and charity shops, said Save the Children's Meek-O'Connor. Pre-loved items are usually what "kids have grown out of quickly rather than things that are poor quality", she said.Image source, Getty ImagesParents can cheaply stock up on frequent-wear items with supermarket bundle deals, while the charity Family Action suggested they team up to bulk buy items that would otherwise take them over budget.According to research from the bank Nationwide, a third of parents said they buy uniform from supermarkets, a third shop around for the best value and 23% purchase larger sizes so items last longer.Kate Steere, parent and consumer editor at the comparison site Finder, said sports kit costs can be "brutal"."I always encourage parents to tap into their club's community. Families with older kids are usually eager to pass down gear," she said."My boys' football team runs a summer sale for second-hand kit, and apps like Vinted or Facebook Marketplace are goldmines."Check for council grantsYou may be able to get a grant from your local authority if your income is below a certain threshold or you're receiving certain benefits.These can be worth up to £200 per child. Eligibility and how much you can get can vary according to where in the UK you live, so it is best to check with your council directly.Struggling with uniform costs is common and people shouldn't feel ashamed if they need to ask for help, said Meek-O'Connor. "Uniform is supposed to be about making school kind of more accessible, more equal...  it should be something positive," she said.Get in touchAre you affected by issues covered in this story?Get our flagship newsletter with all the headlines you need to start the day. Sign up here.

schema.headline: Back to school: How parents can save on uniform costs

title: Nicotine vapes best chance to quit smoking, major review finds
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByMichelle RobertsDigital health editorSmokers who want to quit have the best chance of doing so if they use nicotine e-ciga
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByMichelle RobertsDigital health editorSmokers who want to quit have the best chance of doing so if they use nicotine e-cigarettes, a review has found. The Cochrane team looked at 80 major trials involving nearly 30,000 people and found that nicotine vapes were more effective than traditional aids such as patches, gum and support plans - increasing the success rate by about 60%, from around six in every 100 managing to quit smoking to one in every 10.They outperformed non-nicotine vapes too, although researchers say switching to these afterwards might help with weaning off nicotine.And they could prove more effective than the new anti-smoking pill cytisine, external, which the NHS has started to roll out - although more research is needed.Long-term risks not yet clear Experts say vaping, although not entirely risk-free, is far safer than smoking. In the UK, there are now more over-16s using vapes or e-cigarettes than smoking cigarettes, figures show. Around 5.3 million people or 10% of adults say they smoke, while around 5.4 million use vapes daily or occasionally.The review, external of the most recent and best quality evidence to date applies to regulated vapes that are checked for quality and compliant with strict safety laws. It doesn't look at unregulated ones that can contain illicit substances, like spice or THC. One of the report authors, Dr Jamie Hartmann-Boyce, cautioned: "Unlicensed e-cigarettes are potentially dangerous, with issues including unstable batteries and harmful chemicals. "Anyone looking to use e-cigarettes to quit smoking should only purchase devices that have been tested and approved by their country's regulatory body."The review found no evidence of any increased risk of serious harm from using e-cigarettes to quit.The long-term risks of vaping are not yet clear though, and the NHS says children and non-smokers should never vape. Doctors say vaping could lead to health harms in children and should be made "less attractive" to them. Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Smoking is the leading cause of preventable disease and death, killing over seven million a yearAround two in three people who smoke long-term will die from a tobacco-related illness, says the charity Action on Smoking and Health. According to the World Health Organization, smoking is the leading cause of preventable disease and death, killing over seven million people a year. Quitting smoking reduces your risk of serious illnesses like heart disease, lung cancer, and stroke. Almost every local NHS stop smoking service provides vapes or other support to help people quit.You can search online, external for your local service with your postcode. Get in touchHave you has success quitting smoking by using e-cigarettes?

schema.headline: Nicotine vapes best chance to quit smoking, major review finds

title: Household energy bills to hit three-year high as Ofgem announces 4% rise from October
description: Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh said the removal of VAT on energy bills for six months from October was a "down payment" on helping households with
body: Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh said the removal of VAT on energy bills for six months from October was a "down payment" on helping households with energy costs.She said bills would be £45 less than they would have been and the warm homes discount would take £150 off bills for six million households this winter."We know people are under huge amounts of pressure due to the cost of living, and I know that people are really worried about their energy bills, and we are absolutely alongside them and trying to do everything we can," she told BBC's Today programme.But analysts at the energy consultancy Cornwall Insight have forecast domestic energy prices may rise a further 9% in the new year, bringing renewed concern to households at the coldest time of the year.Shadow energy secretary Claire Coutinho said the government had to "put cheap energy first"."Labour promised to cut energy bills by £300, but they have gone up by nearly £400 instead," she said.Liberal Democrat spokesperson for energy and net zero Pippa Heylings said: "The prime minister must wake up to the scale of the challenge and accept that bold change is needed to bring bills down."Former Prime Minister Gordon Brown also weighed into the issue, saying the government should introduce a "machine gaming tax" and use the proceeds to help those struggling with energy bills.Longer term, he said the government should look at a social tariff for energy."I think Andy Burnham, I know him well, will want to do something along the lines I'm suggesting", he said.Neil Kenward, Ofgem's director general for markets, said while gas bills were rising by 8%, electricity bills were actually falling slightly due to the government's VAT cut."So we are now seeing for the second price cap in a row a bit of a gap open up between gas bills and electricity bills, and that in a sense is positive because it means the transition for example to heat pumps becomes cheaper for households," he told BBC's Today programme.Around 35% of households - or 11 million households - are on fixed tariffs already, but 22 million in England, Wales and Scotland are on tariffs affected by the price cap.Ofgem said the price cap will rise by £60 per year – or £5 per month – to £1,723 for the average household using both electricity and gas if this level was sustained for a year.Kenward said: "Savings are available by choosing a fixed tariff, which are available at £100 or more below the October price cap."The energy cap sets a maximum price for each unit of gas and electricity, not the total bill, so a household's final bill depends on what they use.In July, Ofgem reduced what it believes to be a "typical" level of energy use, because many homes have cut back owing to high prices of recent years while energy efficiency has improved.Its new estimate is 9,500 kWh of gas and 2,500 kWh of electricity a year.Single mum Dana Lazarevic contacted BBC News Your Voice over the difficulties facing people with the cost of living.She says she carefully coordinates washing times to make use of cheaper periods of energy from her supplier at the weekend.Although the lecturer, who lives in Leeds, said that she was not on the breadline, the cost of essentials meant restricting some activities for her children."When winter comes and the cold bites, you need to put on the heating and need to have the money to pay for it," she said. With the cost of each unit of energy higher than at least the last two winters, Jenny Wilson, from Winsford in Cheshire, said everyone is again going to have to tighten their belts."Bills were high enough and bad enough last winter. It was hard for a lot of people," she said.With her family eating ice creams in the warm August weather, she said: "We have made the most of the summer!"The price rise has been driven by wholesale costs, which make up just over a third of a domestic dual-fuel energy bill.The average price of gas has been 61% higher over the past three months compared to late 2025, according to suppliers' trade body Energy UK.Millions of people have moved on to fixed energy tariffs, some in response to the uncertainty created by the impact of the US-Israeli war with Iran.But households are still paying hundreds of pounds a year more on average than before Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 started the energy crisis. Bills have gone up by about 70% compared with the pre-crisis norm, according to industry data.That means unpaid bills and charges have shot up. Energy UK estimates total debt to have collectively risen to £6bn, with an expectation of it to increase to about £7bn by the end of the year.The average billpayer in debt, without a payment plan, owed £3,500, it said.The trade body has called for a flexible discounted tariff for those most in need, funded by taxation. That is supported by many debt charities.

schema.headline: Household energy bills to hit three-year high as Ofgem announces 4% rise from October

title: Father's house was rammed by car before son died in A66 crash
description: A house rammed by a car before the fatal A66 crash in Middlesbrough belonged to the father of a teenager who died in the incident.Cole Worthy, 17, was
body: A house rammed by a car before the fatal A66 crash in Middlesbrough belonged to the father of a teenager who died in the incident.Cole Worthy, 17, was one of five young men who died when a Volkswagen Passat travelling in the wrong direction hit a Cleveland Police armed response vehicle, also killing two police officers.Before the crash at 03:39 BST on Saturday, police had received multiple reports of two cars driving dangerously around the town and a Volvo XC60 was seen ramming properties.The BBC understands that, after his father's home was rammed, Worthy and the four others set out in the Passat. Police said they were linking the activities of the Volvo XC60 and the Passat.There is no suggestion Worthy's father was involved in criminal activity.PC Tom Clough, 38, and PC Matthew Blades, 37, died in the crash, as did Michael Robert Cahill, 23, Jacob Matusiak, 23, Makai Saddington, 18, Theo Rae, 17, and Worthy.The Independent Office for Police Conduct said officers had been pursuing the Passat for almost seven minutes after it was connected to earlier alleged criminal activity, but the pursuit was abandoned 10 seconds before the crash when it turned on to the dual carriageway.Both vehicles were operating with cloned number plates but were picked up by automated number plate recognition technology.

schema.headline: Father's house was rammed by car before son died in A66 crash

title: Newcastle transfer news: Club agree £52m deal for Man City midfielder Nico Gonzalez
description: Although Newcastle's young side came within seconds of defeating Liverpool on the opening weekend, there was always going to be work to do before the
body: Although Newcastle's young side came within seconds of defeating Liverpool on the opening weekend, there was always going to be work to do before the window shut on 1 September.Newcastle have made six signings so far this summer in goalkeepers Lukas Hornicek and Ewen Jaouen, defender Amar Dedic, midfielders Aladji Bamba and Sean Steur and forward Bazoumana Toure.But Jaissle made it clear that "adjustments need to be done and will be" in an interview with BBC Sport last week.After reluctantly selling talisman Guimaraes to Arsenal, Gonzalez possesses the qualities Newcastle have been looking for in the middle of the park.This is a player who would have been potentially out of reach not so long ago.Of those midfielders who played a minimum of 900 minutes in Europe's top five leagues last season, Gonzalez led the way for high turnovers per game (2.13).He also ranked in the Premier League's top five midfielders for line-breaking passes per match (12).Those traits - in and out of possession - could make Gonzalez an invaluable addition as he is handed a greater role at St James' Park.

schema.headline: Newcastle transfer news: Club agree £52m deal for Man City midfielder Nico Gonzalez

title: Chinese teens are turning to mind-numbing drugs to 'run away from reality'
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Buckling under exam pressure, teens in China are turning to prescription drugsByLaura BickerChina corresponde
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Buckling under exam pressure, teens in China are turning to prescription drugsByLaura BickerChina correspondentReporting fromBeijing At 14, *Xiaomei, a high-performing student from a coastal province in China, decided to overdose on cough medication.She wanted to impress an older boy who told her it would help her relax. The tablets were usually only available with a doctor's prescription, but she managed to buy them online.At first she found that they made her a bit dizzy. But she was soon hooked to the slightly numb sensation, which, to her, felt like a brief respite from the pressure of looming exams. When taken in large doses, the drug can cause serious side effects, including hallucinations and impaired coordination.Eventually she tried other medication recommended to her on chat groups. Some were for pain or epileptic seizures. Sometimes she would take five tablets. Other times she would try more than 10 to feel the effects of different drugs.For two years, she took large quantities of various prescription drugs. None of them were prescribed to her or anyone in her family. She bought them all on the internet."When I felt too much pressure from my studies, or I didn't do well at exams, or even when I quarrelled with my parents, I would take these drugs," she told the BBC. "I was running away from reality."The BBC has heard similar stories from dozens of Chinese teenagers in chat rooms across various social media platforms. Nearly every one of them seemed to be escaping the same thing: pressure. They were doing that by chasing what is being described as a "pharmaceutical high".One girl shared a voice note after taking large doses of a neuropathic pain drug. Her words were slurred and hard to comprehend: "I feel my body doesn't belong to me. I'm so dizzy." “Just sleep," comes the advice. "You will be fine tomorrow."One boy offered to use his father's old prescription to fake a new one for the same drug. Some offered tips: "If you want to hallucinate, you can just buy... it's not been controlled yet," says one user,  suggesting a drug used by people with Parkinson's to control tremors. In excessive doses it can cause confusion or even delirium. "Which keyword should I use to search for it on online platforms," another user asks. Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Chinese students spend so much of their day studying, which experts believe only adds to their anxietyIt is hard to gauge the scale of the problem, as there are few official figures. But it is serious enough that the government launched a nationwide crackdown two years ago against the cough suppressant Xiaomei started using, classifying it as a psychotropic drug which would only be available to patients with a doctor's prescription. That made it much harder for young people to buy online. Then in April this year, authorities noticed that young people had switched to another drug and imposed tighter controls on how it is prescribed and dispensed at chemists. Still the BBC was offered the drug in an online chat room for as little as 10 Chinese yuan ($1.5; £1.09) per gram.Non-regulated substances are easy to acquire and even when one drug is controlled by the authorities, young people quickly find alternatives, according to a 2025 paper written for the Crime Prevention Institute at the Ministry of Justice. In some cases the BBC found that teens online were using different names for drugs to avoid detection, which the 2025 study also noted.There is growing evidence that young people across the world are turning to prescription medication to fight off pressures and anxiety. So easy access to cheap prescription drugs in China is perhaps not that surprising given that it produces the vast majority of the world's pharmaceutical ingredients.When Xiaomei wanted to buy the cough suppressant, it just took a few clicks for an entire box of the medication to be delivered at her door, she says. "You could simply enter your ID number on shopping platforms and buy it directly." The ID, which is a national identity number, includes her age but she says she was still sold the drug, no questions asked. It was also cheap - often 50 tablets cost less than a dollar. On paper, China is winning the war on illegal drugs. Official data for 2025 shows a dramatic fall - 41% - in newly identified drug users under the age of 35. However authorities have had to acknowledge that the misuse of prescription drugs is becoming a widespread problem. It has been especially surging among minors, China's National Narcotics Control Commission warned in a recent report.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Students practise yoga to relieve stress before the competitive annual college entrance exam Xiaomei says that a lot of students in her elite chemistry class were discussing ways to overdose on prescription drugs to avoid feeling like "complete losers"."It is just so hard to pass exams and to stay in elite classes. In our school, the elite classes operate on an elimination system; if your academic scores drop, you get kicked out of the class. When you fail, you feel like failures, believing you have no chance in life."Part of the pressure comes from parents who also see their child as their only hope for the future, says renowned Chinese sociologist and director of the Max Planck Institute for Social Anthropology, Xiang Biao.Because of the one-child policy which ended in 2016 after decades, many families only have one child, Biao adds, who shoulders all their expectations."What makes Chinese teens different is their isolating environment. They spend at least nine or 10 hours in school. They have very few chances to develop social relationships, very few opportunities to witness what life is really like."More worrying, he sees a link between prescription drug abuse and an increase in self-harm. The BBC noticed, for instance, that in many of the chat rooms, young people would encourage one another to cut themselves "to feel something".Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Driving up the pressure are parents who see their child as their only hope for the future, experts say As an extremely competitive high school entrance exam drew close, Xiaomei tried a different drug, searching for ways to numb the anxiety."But my memory deteriorated rapidly," she says. "I couldn't remember anything clearly, and I lived in a constant daze." The drug is usually prescribed to help control epileptic seizures and it works as neuropathic pain medication. When Xiaomei explained the side effects in one of her chat groups, they suggested another drug, which is given as pain relief. She says it gave her some release but she soon needed higher doses.Months before sitting the important exam, she went too far. She'd taken 50 tablets and started to panic. "I was afraid something serious might happen, but I didn't want to have my stomach pumped so I wanted to wait before telling my parents."But she became so unwell that she had to confess. Her parents decided to listen to what they saw as their daughter's cry for help. "They mostly expressed how heartbreaking it was for them to see me like that. They didn't scold or criticise me. Their approach was gentle."For her, this has made all the difference."Many children receive lots of attention but the type of attention they want is to be asked how they feel. Do they feel lonely or stressed? Often in China parents brush that away and say you just have to be stronger," Biao says."There's a very loud alarm being sounded out across Chinese society. Adults have to examine how to be responsible for a teenager. Having an open conversation as a family - that is probably the most rewarding part of life."And that is where the real battle lies, according to experts. Rather than playing whack-a-mole trying to suppress online sales of prescription drugs, the government should focus on what may well be a mental health crisis, they say.In 2023, a study for China's Mental Health Blue Book found that nearly 95 million people suffer from depression and more than 30% were under 18 years old.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Competitive exams are a regular feature of teen life in China  The Chinese government has recognised the need for mental health support for teens. Those plans include counselling rooms in every school, psychiatric services in at least one hospital in every county and more mental health professionals. The aim is to build a nationwide system of psychological support and crisis intervention by 2030.So far they have been quite successful. According to the State Council, 92% of primary schools and 95% of junior middle schools now have a counsellor. Many major cities, including Beijing, have started to incorporate mental health into the curriculum.However, there is still a major shortage of medical psychiatrists specialising in children and adolescents. A 2020 study published in British medical journal The Lancet claimed there were only 500 qualified child psychiatrists in the country, and many of them were based in major cities such as Beijing and Shanghai.This is a huge challenge in a country that has undergone three decades of unprecedented social and economic change. The China Xiaomei's parents grew up in is very different from the future she is facing. Her parents followed a script set by the Communist Party: work hard and you will be rewarded. Now, even if young adults pass with high grades and get a university degree, a bright future is not guaranteed.Following gruelling pandemic restrictions, the Chinese economy has struggled to bounce back. One in five young people are thought to be struggling to find a job and families are spending less."People have become more pessimistic in general," Biao admits. And the anxiety extends to adults, he adds."I think parents feel confused and anxious because they see a problem in their children, but they don't see an alternative. If my child has a problem, it's the end of the world. If my child doesn't do well in school, it's the end of the world. If my child doesn't speak to me, it's the end of the world. I think we should pay more attention to parents as well as children."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Listening to teens and having open conversations with them is essential, according to mental health experts Fortunately Xiaomei and her parents have managed to find a way to cross this bridge."In the past, my parents didn't really understand me and would say some pretty harsh things. I felt like I had no help and was truly on my own," she says.But that changed when she was rushed to hospital after the overdose. They started listening to her and talking to her, and "knowing that there was someone standing by my side made me feel really good", she says. It even helped her perform well in the entrance exam she had been dreading for so long."I am lucky to have their support," she adds.Not everyone finds such support though, and that's where *Lu Jingchan hopes he can help.The 22-year-old spent years battling depression. He found it hard to beat the euphoria that came from taking prescription drugs, and overdosed more than four times in four years."The drugs drove me to the brink of madness. You risk sinking into an abyss of addiction, destroying your health," he says.He has now quit all prescription medication, and spends his time on social media urging others not to start. And he has this advice for young people battling the pressures he once did."I hope you can face life head-on, without needing medicines to numb yourselves. If you are overdosing, I want to give you the courage to stop. I believe your lives will improve. I believe you will all find happiness."*Names have been changed to protect their identity

schema.headline: Chinese teens are turning to mind-numbing drugs to 'run away from reality'

title: US Open 2026: Serena Williams and Carlos Alcaraz return in mixed doubles
description: Enjoy it - and do what Serena Williams tells you to.That was how Carlos Alcaraz settled back into competitive action at the US Open, partnering the Am
body: Enjoy it - and do what Serena Williams tells you to.That was how Carlos Alcaraz settled back into competitive action at the US Open, partnering the American great as she returned to her home slam after a four-year absence.The tournament's revamped mixed doubles format has attracted criticism for favouring the allure of the sport's top singles stars at the expense of established doubles players.But the crowds turned out and produced a terrific atmosphere for the tournament's headline act, with about 15,000 people packed inside Arthur Ashe Stadium.All four doubles specialist pairings lost to a team of singles players on Tuesday, while Alcaraz and Williams fell in the quarter-finals.Seven-time major winner Alcaraz was playing his first competitive match since April after injuring his wrist, while 23-time Grand Slam champion Williams was competing in New York for the first time since she "evolved away" from tennis in 2022.The pair were greeted by huge cheers and were roared on throughout their opening 5-3 4-1 win against Great Britain's Lloyd Glasspool and New Zealand's Erin Routliffe.The 44-year-old Williams won the US Open mixed doubles title in its original format alongside Max Mirnyi in 1998 - five years before Alcaraz was born.Almost 30 years later, Williams still had the competitive desire. She and Alcaraz enjoyed the occasion, playing with smiles on their faces and roaring each other on after winning a point.Interviewed during a change of ends, Alcaraz said: "I'm playing next to the one and only Serena Williams, so what else can I do? Just enjoy and try to do the things she told me to do."Their partnership improved rapidly in their first match as they won eight of the final nine games to seal victory.However, they were denied a place in Wednesday's semi-finals by Italy's world number six Flavio Cobolli and Swiss team-mate Belinda Bencic, who won 5-4 (7-4) 4-1.While Williams will not contest the singles at the US Open - she has not competed in that format since injuring her knee at Wimbledon - Tuesday's matches provided the returning Alcaraz with valuable court time.The Spaniard admitted he felt nervous before stepping out on the court - in part due to partnering six-time US Open women's singles champion Williams."I think everyone could see I was really nervous, I double-faulted on the first point," Alcaraz said after their opening win."I was out for almost five months and I almost forgot how it feels stepping out on the court once again. "It [took] just a couple of games [to settle] and she made it very easy for me to enjoy it and try to go for it."For Williams, a return to the Arthur Ashe Stadium was something she did not believe would come around again."It's always amazing to be here. I never expected to be back on this court," Williams said."It was just a really cool moment. I never thought this would happen."The controversial revamped mixed doubles format, introduced last year, pits established doubles players against some of the sport's biggest singles stars.The tournament takes place the week before the singles draw gets under way and allows direct entry into the main draw for top-ranked singles players and wildcards.Established doubles players such as Britons Glasspool and Henry Patten had to come through two qualifying rounds on Monday.Top-ranked players Patten and Katerina Siniakova advanced to the quarter-finals before losing to husband-and-wife duo Gael Monfils and Elina Svitolina.Discussing their dynamic, with a semi-final against Cobolli and Bencic to come, Frenchman Monfils said: "I'm a big fan of her game and mentality. Sometimes I think she's ice and I'm the fire."We needed to the find the balance. We did today."The other semi-final will see Russians Mirra Andreeva and Andrey Rublev face Czech pair Karolina Muchova and Jakub Mensik.It was not all plain sailing for the leading singles players, with men's 24-time major winner Novak Djokovic and women's world number one Aryna Sabalenka suffering an early exit at the hands of Patten and Siniakova.

schema.headline: US Open 2026: Serena Williams and Carlos Alcaraz return in mixed doubles

title: Michael Sheen toxic waste documentary 'the tip of the iceberg'
description: A former Monsanto worker who spent three years helping seal toxic waste underground said staff had "cheap" protective equipment and were not told what
body: A former Monsanto worker who spent three years helping seal toxic waste underground said staff had "cheap" protective equipment and were not told what they were burying.Stephen Constance worked at the chemical giant's Newport factory in the 1990s and came forward after the BBC documentary Buried with Michael Sheen highlighted Wales' toxic waste legacy.But the 14 sites identified in the programme are just the tip of the iceberg and there are about 20,000 high-concern sites in the UK, said Dr David Megson, the scientist involved in the documentary.Eastman Chemical Company, which is responsible for Monsanto's legacy production in the UK, did not respond when asked to comment.Constance was one of dozens of people who contacted BBC Wales after coverage of Sheen's investigation into Monsanto and the dumping of polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs).Researcher and whistleblower Douglas Gowan spent 50 years trying to persuade authorities to investigate what he believed was widespread dumping of industrial chemicals.These included PCBs, which he called "some of the worst contaminants known to man", and were widely used in the 20th Century, including for lipstick and white goods.They were banned in the UK in the 1970s and have since been banned by 151 countries.Dr Megson, a reader in chemistry and environmental forensics at Manchester Metropolitan University, led the scientific data collection in the documentary.He said: "The country is in a really dire place."Public pressure is the only thing that's going to make this action happen. This is our only chance, if I'm being brutally honest."What our data shows is those sites are leaking and those sites are a chemical cocktail. Whether it's the PCBs alone is up for debate."PCBs are suspected carcinogens, so we think they can cause cancer."The data he found stunned him after having met people who had been worried about PCB levels near their family home for more than 30 years, saying he found levels that were "pretty much the highest I've ever seen in anything we've tested".He added: "It's made me feel quite uncomfortable about some of those sites and what could have happened to all of those people's friends and loved ones."The polluter just keeps getting away with stuff left, right and centre."A report by an environmental engineering consultancy in 2006, seen by BBC Wales, shows that the acid tar lagoon - one of the sites in the documentary - was known to be contaminated as early as 1979. Among the known contaminants dumped at the site is 93,100 tonnes of acid sludge from Burmah Castrol and barrels of unknown substances suspected to be from Monsanto, the report said.Over the next 27 years, there were 18 investigations, two remediation proposals and five treatment trials but, as of 2026, the acid tar lagoon remains. The report identified 105 possible ways contamination from the site could affect people, wildlife, property or water supplies.This included three uncapped mine shafts beneath the lagoon that were suggested as potential pathways for contaminant movement.  In the 1980s, Clwyd County Council bought the site and legally agreed to protect the previous owner from any past, present or future claims, costs or liabilities arising from the "escape or nuisance of noxious wastes".BP, which is responsible for Burmah Castrol, said it had no comment to make.John Browne, a lawyer specialising in industrial disease claims at Slater and Gordon, said cases involving historical contamination were difficult to investigate - but not impossible."Time passing makes cases more difficult to prove," he said."Witnesses' memories fade and locating [eye]witnesses becomes increasingly challenging and difficult."However, he said scientific, medical and forensic evidence could help establish what happened and whether exposure to hazardous substances contributed to illness.The key question is not simply what the law was at the time, but what was known about the risks, he said, adding: "Communities affected by contamination deserve transparency and clear answers."Public Health Wales said its Welsh cancer intelligence and surveillance unit had collected and analysed "every single case of cancer" since the 1970s.It added: "Based on the evidence currently available, there is no indication that historical environmental pollution is responsible for an increased risk of cancer, or any other disease or illness, in these areas."Natural Resources Wales said the Environment Agency, its predecessor, investigated the acid tar lake in 2006 and 2008 but tests concluded it did not meet the legal definition of contaminated land."Therefore, responsibility for the site returned and remains with Wrexham County Council as regulator."Wrexham council said, since these investigations 20 years ago, ongoing monitoring had not identified any significant changes and there was no statutory requirement for remediation.The Welsh government said addressing contaminated land was one of its key priorities. "A survey of local authorities carried out by Natural Resources Wales in 2015 identified more than 9,000 potential sites requiring further investigation. "While not all of these sites will pose a risk to human health or the environment, this figure demonstrates the scale of the issue facing regulators in Wales."We now intend to develop a Wales-wide strategy to progressively restore post-industrial land, so that communities are no longer exposed to potential risks."The UK government referred the BBC to the Welsh government when asked to comment.
